Since you have an interest in DIY electronics and are already familiar with the Raspberry Pi ecosystem, using two cameras to create a high-resolution "stitched" image is a very achievable project.

The Raspberry Pi 5 is your best candidate here because it features two CSI (Camera Serial Interface) ports, allowing you to connect and trigger two high-resolution cameras simultaneously.

1. Recommended Hardware

To get the best resolution for reading text on a large board, I recommend the Raspberry Pi High Quality (HQ) Camera.

  • Sensor: 12.3-megapixel Sony IMX477.
  • Lenses: You can choose a wide-angle lens (e.g., 6mm) to capture more area per camera, or a telephoto lens if the camera needs to be far away.
  • Interface: Two HQ cameras connected to the two ports on a Raspberry Pi 5.

2. The Capture and Stitching Workflow

The process involves two main steps: capturing the raw frames and then "stitching" them into a single image using software.

Step A: Synchronized Capture

You can use libcamera (the modern RPi camera stack) to trigger both cameras at once.

# Capture from camera 0 (Left)
libcamera-still --camera 0 -o left.jpg
# Capture from camera 1 (Right)
libcamera-still --camera 1 -o right.jpg

Step B: Automated Stitching with OpenCV

Since you enjoy technical projects, you can use a Python script with the OpenCV library to merge these images. OpenCV has a built-in Stitcher class that automatically detects overlapping features and aligns the photos.

import cv2

# Load the two images
images = [cv2.imread('left.jpg'), cv2.imread('right.jpg')]

# Initialize OpenCV's stitching tool
stitcher = cv2.Stitcher_create()
status, stitched_image = stitcher.stitch(images)

if status == cv2.Stitcher_OK:
    cv2.imwrite('final_board_scan.jpg', stitched_image)
    print("Stitch successful!")
else:
    print(f"Stitching failed with status code {status}")

3. Tips for a Clean Stitch

  • Overlap: Ensure the two cameras have about 30–50% overlap in their field of view. This gives the software enough "anchor points" to align the text perfectly.
  • Fixed Mount: Since you want to do this every 24 hours, use a T-bar mount or a custom 3D-printed bracket to keep the cameras at a fixed angle.
  • Lighting: Consistency is key. If the building's lights change, use a fixed exposure setting in your script so both halves of the image have the same brightness.

4. Alternative: The "No-Code" Way

If you'd rather not write a stitching script, you can have the Pi upload the two raw images to a folder on your computer and use PhotoStitcher or Hugin. These are GUI-based tools that can take a batch of images and output a high-res panorama with one click.

In photography, exposure and resolution are two different "levers." A long exposure allows a sensor to gather more light (improving clarity in the dark), but it won't physically add more pixels to the sensor to capture fine text.

However, since you're looking for a cheaper, technical alternative that mimics a "high-end" scan using lower-cost hardware, you should look into Computational Super-Resolution.

1. The "Synthetic" High-Resolution Alternative

Instead of one expensive 12MP sensor, you can use a cheap 5MP sensor (like the Raspberry Pi Camera V1 or V2) and take a burst of 10–20 images at slightly different angles or "jittered" positions.

  • How it works: This is called Multi-Frame Super-Resolution. By combining multiple low-res shots, an algorithm can "fill in" the gaps between pixels to create a final image with much higher detail than the hardware technically supports.
  • The Hardware: A single Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W + a cheap V2 Camera (~$25–$30 total).
  • The Logic: You use a script to take 10 photos in rapid succession. Even tiny vibrations in the building or slight "noise" in the sensor provide enough variation for the software to reconstruct a sharper image.

Since you enjoy DIY electronics, you could build a Line-Scan Camera or a "Wall Scanner" using a motorized rail.

  • The Concept: Rather than trying to capture the whole board at once, you mount a cheap camera on a linear actuator (stepper motor + lead screw or belt).
  • The Workflow:
    1. The Pi triggers the motor to move the camera across a rail.
    2. The camera takes "strips" of the board as it moves.
    3. Software (like OpenCV or Hugin) stitches these vertical strips into one massive, extremely high-resolution image.
  • Cost: You can find cheap stepper motors and rails for ~$30. Combined with a $10 camera, you get a resolution that would cost $500+ in a single lens.

3. Use an Old Smartphone with a "Super-Res" App

    3. Auto-sync the photo to your Google Drive.

turns.prompt_text: How would you build the Gantry to do that?
turns.response_html:
Building a gantry (the framework for a moving camera) is a classic mechanical engineering challenge. Since you are in Ankeny and have ties to the Iowa State community, you’re in a great spot to find parts—Ames has plenty of maker resources.

To build a "Wall Scanner," you basically need to build one axis of a 3D printer, but stretched out to the width of your board.

1. The Physical Framework (The Rail)

You need a "track" for the phone to slide along.

  • V-Slot Aluminum Extrusions: These are the gold standard for DIY gantries. They are lightweight, rigid, and have a groove for wheels to roll in. You can buy these in lengths up to 2 meters.
  • The Carriage: This is the "sled" that holds your phone. It uses three or four Delrin V-wheels that tension into the grooves of the aluminum rail.

2. The Motion System (The Drive)

To move the carriage across the wall, you have two main options:

  • GT2 Timing Belt (Recommended): This is what most 3D printers use. You mount a NEMA 17 Stepper Motor at one end and an idler pulley at the other. The belt loops around and attaches to the carriage. It’s fast, quiet, and very accurate.
  • Lead Screw: More powerful but slower. A long threaded rod spins, and a nut attached to your carriage moves it along. For a wide board, a lead screw might "whip" (vibrate) too much. Stick with a belt.

3. The Electronics (The Brains)

Since you’ve worked with Raspberry Pi Picos, you can use one to control the motor.

  • Controller: Raspberry Pi Pico or an Arduino.
  • Motor Driver: An A4988 or TMC2209 driver. This acts as the middleman between your Pico and the motor to provide the necessary current.
  • Limit Switches: You need a small "endstop" switch at the "Home" position. This tells the Pico where the camera is so it doesn't try to drive the phone through the wall.

4. The "Scan" Logic

Instead of a continuous video, you want the gantry to perform a "Step and Shoot" routine:

  1. Home: Move to the far left until it hits the limit switch.
  2. Position 1: Move to the first "zone," stop, and trigger the phone (you can trigger the phone via Bluetooth or a simple timed delay).
  3. Position 2: Move 2 feet to the right, stop, and trigger.
  4. Repeat: Continue until the end of the board is reached.
  5. Return: Slide back to the start to wait for the next 24-hour cycle.

5. Budget Materials List

Gantry Plate + Wheels$15Standard 3D printer replacement parts
NEMA 17 Stepper Motor$12Very common, check eBay/Amazon
GT2 Belt & Pulley Kit$10Look for "3D printer motion kits"
A4988 Driver$5Usually comes in packs of 5

How to Trigger the Phone?

Since you're using a phone on the gantry, the easiest way to tell the phone to "take the picture" when the gantry stops is a Bluetooth Camera Shutter. You can take a $5 Bluetooth remote, crack it open, and wire the "button" to one of the pins on your Raspberry Pi Pico. When the Pico finishes moving the motor, it "presses" the button electronically.

turns.prompt_text: would it be easier just to swivel the phone
turns.response_html:
Swiveling the phone is definitely easier to build than a linear gantry, but it comes with a trade-off in image quality and geometry.

Since you are dealing with a large board on a flat wall, here is how a swivel (Pan-Tilt) system compares to a sliding (Gantry) system:

1. The "Ease of Build" Advantage

Swiveling is much simpler because it only requires one or two motors in a fixed location. You don't need to buy long aluminum rails, belts, or rollers.

  • The Hardware: You can use two high-torque servo motors or small stepper motors (like the 28BYJ-48) and a 3D-printed or cardboard mount.
  • The Movement: The camera stays in one spot and "scans" the wall by rotating.

2. The "Geometry" Problem

This is the main hurdle. When you slide a camera along a wall (Gantry), the distance to the board stays the same, keeping the text size and focus consistent. When you swivel:

  • Keystone Distortion: The text in the center of the board will look normal, but text at the far left and right will look "stretched" and slanted because the camera is seeing it at an angle.
  • Focus Issues: The edges of the board are further away from the camera than the center. You’ll need to ensure your phone’s autofocus is fast or set a deep depth of field so everything stays legible.

3. How to Make Swiveling Work

If you choose the swivel route, you can fix the distortion using software:

  • Spherical Stitching: Use a tool like Hugin or Adobe Lightroom/Photoshop. These programs understand that the photos were taken from a single point and "project" them onto a flat plane, automatically fixing the slanting text.
  • The "Nodal Point" Trick: For the best results, try to mount the phone so it rotates around the center of its lens (the nodal point), not the center of the phone body. This prevents "parallax" errors where things don't line up perfectly in the overlap.

Comparison: Swivel vs. Gantry

FeatureSwivel (Pan-Tilt)Gantry (Slider)
Mechanical SetupVery Easy (1-2 motors)Complex (Rail, Belts, Carriage)
Space RequiredMinimalMust be as wide as the board
Image QualityGood (but requires stitching)Excellent (true "flat" scan)
Best For...Budget builds / Small roomsMaximum legibility of fine print

Which is better for you?

If the text on the board is large and clear, a swivel is much more practical. If you're trying to read tiny, dense handwriting or math equations from across the room, the Gantry will provide the pixel-perfect clarity you need across the entire surface.

Given your interest in DIY electronics and your Iowa State background, you might find building the swivel a faster "win" to test the concept before committing to a full-wall rail system.

Instead of using the phone's native "Panorama" mode, your Raspberry Pi Pico will tell the swivel mount to move to three or four specific angles. At each angle, the phone takes a standard high-res photo.

  • Angle A (Left): Snap.
  • Angle B (Center): Snap.
  • Angle C (Right): Snap.

This ensures you get the full sensor resolution for every section of the board, which is much sharper than a single "swept" panorama.

2. Correcting the "Swivel Distortions"

Because the camera is rotating from a single point, the "Left" and "Right" photos will have Keystone Distortion (the text looks slanted or "squashed" at the edges).

The DIY Software Fix: OpenCV

Since you're comfortable with technical projects, you can use a Python script on your home computer (or a more powerful Raspberry Pi) to "deskew" these images automatically. You can use a Perspective Transform: $$\begin{bmatrix} x' \ y' \ 1 \end{bmatrix} = H \begin{bmatrix} x \ y \ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Where $H$ is the homography matrix that maps the slanted board back into a perfect rectangle.

3. Automated Stitching Tools

If you don't want to code the math yourself, there are "set it and forget it" tools:

  • Hugin (Free/Open Source): This is the powerhouse for this. You can create a "template." Once you align your first set of photos, you can save that template and use the Hugin Command Line to batch-stitch every new daily photo automatically.
  • Microsoft ICE (Image Composite Editor): If you have an old Windows machine, this is the most "magical" tool—it handles the keystone and stitching with zero configuration.

4. Hardware Tip: The "Nodal Point"

When you build your swivel mount, try to place the phone so that the actual camera lens is directly over the center of the motor's rotation. If the lens is "swinging" in a wide arc, the images won't align perfectly (this is called Parallax Error). Keeping the lens centered makes the stitching software's job 10x easier.

import cv2
import os
import time

# Path to your Google Drive synced folder
IMAGE_FOLDER = "C:/Users/Austin/Google Drive/Board_Scans/"

def auto_stitch():
    # Load all images in the folder
    images = [cv2.imread(os.path.join(IMAGE_FOLDER, f)) for f in os.listdir(IMAGE_FOLDER) if f.endswith(".jpg")]
    
    if len(images) < 2:
        return

    # Initialize OpenCV Stitcher
    stitcher = cv2.Stitcher_create()
    (status, stitched) = stitcher.stitch(images)

    if status == cv2.STITCHER_OK:
        cv2.imwrite("final_board_daily.png", stitched)
        print("Stitch complete!")
        # Optional: Clean out the folder for tomorrow
    else:
        print(f"Stitching failed. Error code: {status}")

# Run this every night at 6 PM
while True:
    auto_stitch()
    time.sleep(86400) # Wait 24 hours

Rooting your TCL phone would give you administrative (superuser) privileges, effectively turning you into a "god user" with total control over every file and system service. While rooting offers the deepest level of control, it is often a "high-risk, high-reward" path for a project like this.

1. What Rooting Specifically Enables

If you were to root the device, you could control it from your computer in ways that standard apps cannot:

  • Complete Remote Automation: You can use a computer to send low-level "shell commands" to simulate touch, keypresses, and system reboots without any security pop-ups.
  • Kernel Control: You can under-volt or under-clock the processor from your PC to save battery life or prevent the phone from overheating while it sits on the wall 24/7.
  • Advanced Power Management: You can use root-level apps like Advanced Charging Controller (ACC) to force the phone to run solely on the charger's power without actually charging the battery, which completely eliminates the risk of the battery swelling from being plugged in constantly.
  • System-Wide Ad & Tracker Blocking: You can install a root-level firewall to ensure the phone never uses data for anything except uploading your board photos.

2. The "PC Control" Reality (Root vs. No-Root)

Interestingly, you don't actually need to root to control the phone from your PC.

  • Scrcpy (No Root Required): This is the "gold standard" for controlling Android from a PC. It mirrors your screen and lets you use your mouse and keyboard to control the phone over USB or Wi-Fi.
  • ADB (Android Debug Bridge): You can send commands from your computer's terminal to take screenshots, install apps, or pull files directly—all without root, as long as USB Debugging is enabled.

3. The Major "TCL" Caveat

Rooting budget phones like those from TCL or Cricket can be extremely difficult.

  • Locked Bootloaders: Many carrier-branded phones (like Cricket) have "locked bootloaders" that prevent you from rooting them at all.
  • Risk of Bricking: If the rooting process fails, it can "brick" the phone, making it permanently unusable.

Would you like me to help you check if your specific TCL model has an unlockable bootloader before you attempt to root it?

Checking if that TCL Cricket phone has an unlockable bootloader is a straightforward process that you can do mostly from the device itself before you even touch a computer.

How to Check Your Bootloader Status

Follow these steps to see if rooting is even an option for your specific model:

  • Enable Developer Options: Go to Settings > System Information > Build Number and tap "Build Number" 7 times until you see a "You are now a developer" message.
  • Check the "OEM Unlocking" Toggle: Go back to Settings > System > Developer Options. Look for a switch labeled "OEM Unlocking".
    • If you can toggle it: Your bootloader can likely be unlocked.
    • If it is grayed out: The bootloader is likely permanently locked by the carrier (Cricket), which is common for budget TCL devices.
  • The Dialing Shortcut: Open the phone dialer and enter *#*#7378423#*#*. If a menu appears, go to Service Info > Configuration to see if "Bootloader unlock allowed" says "Yes".
  • The ADB Test: Connect the phone to a PC with USB Debugging enabled and use the command fastboot oem device-info or fastboot getvar unlocked to see the current status.

No-Root Control Alternatives

If you find the bootloader is locked, don't worry—you can still control the phone almost entirely from your computer using ADB (Android Debug Bridge) and Scrcpy.

  • Scrcpy: Allows you to mirror the phone's screen to your PC and use your mouse/keyboard to operate it exactly as if it were a window on your desktop.
  • Shell Commands: You can send a command like adb shell input tap x y from your PC to take a photo at a specific time without needing the phone to be rooted.

Finding Your Exact Model

To confirm your hardware specs, go to Settings > System > About Phone. You will see the Model Name (e.g., TCL 30 Z) and the Model Number (e.g., T602DL).
